title: Long life: At 93, I miss the Queen more than ever
gist: Actor and writer Sheila Hancock, 93, argues that despite her left-wing egalitarian views she now prefers hereditary monarchy to elected leaders like Trump or Netanyahu, citing Queen Elizabeth's lifelong service and King Charles's address to the US House of Representatives. She frames the monarchy as a stabilising alternative to volatile democratic outcomes such as the Brexit referendum.

insights.claim: Sheila Hancock, a self-described left-wing egalitarian, says hereditary monarchy is infinitely preferable to a country led by elected figures like Trump or Netanyahu.
insights.speaker: Sheila Hancock
insights.so_what: Signals that disillusionment with populist democracy is pushing even progressive voices toward institutional continuity, supporting UK monarchy stability.
insights.quote: I consider having a royal family by inheritance infinitely preferable to ending up with a country led by the elected Trump or Netanyahu
insights.locator: But I am very old now

insights.claim: Hancock distrusts direct citizen decision-making, pointing to low turnout and the 'ruinous' Brexit referendum result as reasons to prefer a trained hereditary head of state until a better system is devised.
insights.speaker: Sheila Hancock
insights.so_what: Reflects lingering elite scepticism of referendums in UK politics, lowering odds of future plebiscite-driven shocks.
insights.quote: I really don’t want the future to be decided by citizens, many of whom don’t bother to vote
insights.locator: But I am very old now

insights.claim: Hancock argues the hereditary system has historically filtered out unsuitable monarchs such as the Duke of Windsor and produced better royals than the UK's elected leaders.
insights.speaker: Sheila Hancock
insights.so_what: A legitimacy argument for monarchy based on comparative performance rather than tradition.
insights.quote: The system seems to get rid of the duds like the Duke of Windsor

insights.claim: A televised programme by John Humphrys, backed by Nicola Sturgeon, made the case for abolishing the royal family, indicating republicanism remains an active debate in UK media in 2026.
insights.speaker: Sheila Hancock
insights.so_what: Republican sentiment has mainstream airtime post-Elizabeth, a slow-burn constitutional risk for the UK.
insights.locator: My life is hurtling towards its end

insights.claim: King Charles addressed the US House of Representatives while receiving cancer treatment, delivering what Hancock calls one of the best political speeches she has heard and an implicit rebuke of Trump's conduct.
insights.speaker: Sheila Hancock
insights.so_what: UK soft power via the monarchy is being deployed in US-UK relations as a counterweight to Trump-era politics.
insights.quote: With immense dignity, he made one of the best political speeches I have ever heard.
insights.locator: While his marital history is lamentable

insights.claim: Charles's speech stressed generosity of spirit, compassion, peace and valuing people of all faiths and none, which Hancock reads as the antithesis of Trump's style.
insights.speaker: Sheila Hancock
insights.so_what: Monarchical messaging positions the UK as a values-based partner distinct from the current US administration.
insights.quote: a duty to foster compassion, to promote peace, to deepen mutual understanding and to value all people of all faiths and of none
insights.locator: While his marital history is lamentable

insights.claim: Hancock credits Queen Elizabeth with meeting virtually every important world figure over 50 years, giving her a uniquely trusted, stabilising presence that made people feel safer.
insights.speaker: Sheila Hancock
insights.so_what: Loss of a stabilising symbolic figure can erode institutional trust, a soft factor in national cohesion.
insights.quote: I felt safer when she was around.

insights.claim: Hancock says the royal family and the world have completely changed in the four years since Queen Elizabeth's death.
insights.speaker: Sheila Hancock
insights.so_what: Frames the post-2022 period as a structural break in UK institutional and global order.
insights.quote: In that time, the royal family—and the world in general—has completely changed.
insights.locator: My life is hurtling towards its end

insights.claim: Hancock closes by urging the UK to think carefully about the next era after the Queen, implying the monarchy's future is an open question.
insights.speaker: Sheila Hancock
insights.so_what: Constitutional future of the UK monarchy remains a live, if slow-moving, political question.
insights.quote: The end of an era. Let us hope we think carefully about the next.
